solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Tribunal date officer announced

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out, so the word before it is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: to date someone is to woo or go out with them, an old sense of court
a marshal is a high-ranking officer; the adjective meaning warlike is said the same way

explanation.surface: A notice giving the date of a hearing, read out by an official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tribunal date' reads as a single phrase about a hearing's schedule, but date is the wordplay and Tribunal stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A court martial is a military judicial body trying members of the armed forces, a kind of tribunal.

clue.text: Unplanned rebuilding of a noted clinic

indicators.note: rebuilding takes something apart and puts it together in a new form, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the twelve letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A well-known clinic gets an unscheduled refurbishment.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder letters are exactly the twelve of 'a noted clinic'; the rest of the clue is the definition and the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something coincidental happens by chance, without design or intention, which is what unplanned describes.

clue.text: Deliver golf club without its head

indicators.note: losing its head means the opening letter of the word is cut away

blocks.note: the putter is the club used on the green

explanation.surface: Handing over a golf club whose head has come off.
explanation.walkthrough: Deliver suggests handing over goods, but here it means delivering words, as in delivering a speech.
explanation.definitionFit: To deliver a remark or speech is to say it aloud, which is the sense of the verb here.

clue.text: One of the social insects, they’re regularly seen with arachnid

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters, ignoring the apostrophe
a mite is a tiny relative of spiders

explanation.surface: Social insects are often found living alongside spiders.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of 'they're' are counted without the apostrophe: T, E, R.
explanation.definitionFit: Termites live in large colonies with castes of workers and soldiers, making them one of the classic social insects alongside ants and bees.

clue.text: Declared Authorized Version outstanding

blocks.note: the first letters of the two words, the usual short name for the King James Bible
an outstanding debt is one still owed

explanation.surface: Someone proclaims the King James Bible to be excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: Outstanding looks like praise for the translation, but it means unpaid. The Authorized Version is the 1611 English Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: Avowed means openly stated or professed, as in an avowed atheist, matching a declared position.

clue.text: Derelict public transport vehicle close to dump

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is taken

blocks.note: a tram runs on rails through city streets
final letter of the word

explanation.surface: An abandoned bus or tram left rotting near the rubbish tip.
explanation.walkthrough: Derelict reads as an adjective describing the vehicle, but it is a noun: a homeless vagrant.
explanation.definitionFit: A derelict as a noun is a destitute, homeless person, which is what a vagrant wanderer is.

clue.text: A serious error in English is foolish

blocks.note: taken as written
a sin is a grave wrong
taken as written
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Making a bad mistake in your English is silly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it places the error inside English, but it is simply its own two letters in sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: Asinine literally means like an ass or donkey, and so stupid or silly.

clue.text: Complete absorption of doorkeepers with time?

blocks.note: read whimsically as the men at the entrance
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Doormen becoming totally engrossed as the hours pass.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that doorkeepers is taken loosely as 'entrance men', not a real phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Entrancement is the state of being held spellbound, a total engrossment of attention.

clue.text: Cold season killing off first plant

indicators.note: killing off the first means the opening letter is removed

blocks.note: the cold season of the year

explanation.surface: A cold spell kills a plant before others.
explanation.walkthrough: Plant looks like a noun for something growing, but it is a verb: to put into the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter is to bury a body, and to plant can mean to bury or set something in the earth.

clue.text: Speech limit after Oscar

blocks.note: Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to ration is to restrict the amount allowed

explanation.surface: Acceptance speeches at the Oscars have a time limit.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads limit then Oscar, but 'after' puts the limit second.
explanation.definitionFit: An oration is a formal address delivered to an audience, a type of speech.

clue.text: Wow! Lovely ornamental moulding

blocks.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise
a plain synonym

explanation.surface: Someone admiring a beautiful decorative plaster feature.
explanation.walkthrough: Cor is everyday British slang for wow.
explanation.definitionFit: A cornice is the decorative band running along the top of a wall where it meets the ceiling.

clue.text: Coming before head of house

blocks.note: first meaning: earlier in time or order
second meaning: the superior of a religious house such as a priory

explanation.surface: Arriving ahead of whoever runs the household.
explanation.walkthrough: House here is a religious community, not a home.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an adjective for something earlier and a noun for the monk who governs a monastery or priory.

clue.text: Wild garden hazard

indicators.note: something wild is disordered and out of control, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An overgrown garden can be a menace.
explanation.walkthrough: Wild reads as describing an overgrown garden, but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A hazard is a source of risk or peril, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Band’s vehicle caught in dreadful rain

indicators.note: something caught in something else is held inside it
dreadful means terribly bad, suggesting letters in a mess

blocks.note: taken as written
a van is a goods vehicle

explanation.surface: A rock group's tour van stuck in a downpour.
explanation.walkthrough: Band's is Band is: the definition is followed by a joining 's. The van goes between NIR and A.
explanation.definitionFit: Nirvana was the Seattle grunge group fronted by Kurt Cobain, an example of a band.

clue.text: A small seabird at the rear of the ship

definitions.text: at the rear of the ship

blocks.note: taken as written
S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
a tern is a slender gull-like seabird

explanation.surface: A little seabird perched at the back of a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the whole clue one picture; the definition is only the last five words.
explanation.definitionFit: Astern is a nautical adverb meaning behind or towards the back end of a vessel.

clue.text: Attention seeker’s reason for returning tickets?

blocks.note: first meaning: a person who flaunts themselves, with 's as is
second meaning, read cryptically: the performance has been cancelled

explanation.surface: Why a person craving the spotlight might hand back their theatre seats.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is whimsical: if a performance is called off you return the tickets, and the question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A show-off is someone who parades their talents to be noticed, while a cancelled performance is one that has been called off.

clue.text: Forcefully hit one in

blocks.note: first meaning: to strike repeatedly and hard
second meaning: the player currently in at the crease in cricket or baseball

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the side batting is 'in', so 'one in' is a player at the wicket.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to pound violently, and the noun is the player facing the bowler or pitcher.

clue.text: Bottle never gets broken

indicators.note: something broken is smashed into pieces that can be put back differently

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A boast that a particular bottle is unbreakable.
explanation.walkthrough: Bottle is British slang for courage, as in 'lose your bottle'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bottle in British slang means courage or daring, the same quality as having the nerve to do something.

clue.text: Force out former performers in light entertainment

blocks.note: ex means formerly, as in ex-wife
a variety act is a performer or troupe on a bill

explanation.surface: Ejecting old-time variety stars from show business.
explanation.walkthrough: Force out reads as eject, but it means to extract a payment or concession, as in exact revenge.
explanation.definitionFit: To exact is to demand and obtain something by pressure, so to extract or wring it out.

clue.text: Peter perhaps brewed top ales

indicators.note: brewing mixes and transforms ingredients, so the letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man named Peter, maybe a home brewer, makes excellent beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks Peter as one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Peter was one of the twelve disciples chosen by Jesus, so an example of the class.

clue.text: Particular thanks in letter from abroad

blocks.note: the definite article points to a particular one
ta is British slang for thank you

explanation.surface: Special gratitude expressed in a note sent from overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it puts one piece inside another, but it is only a joining word. Ta is everyday British for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth character of the Greek alphabet, so a foreign alphabet symbol.

clue.text: First male worker in firm

blocks.note: in Genesis the first man created
the worker ant is a crossword staple

explanation.surface: The first man to be employed by a company.
explanation.walkthrough: Firm reads as a company, but it is the adjective meaning unyielding.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone adamant refuses to be persuaded or change their mind, so is resolute and unbending.

clue.text: Do be serious — that does contain fat

indicators.note: to contain is to hold within, so the letters sit inside the phrase

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words, starting from the last letter of the first

explanation.surface: Someone urging seriousness about whether a food has fat in it.
explanation.walkthrough: The sought letters start at the final letter of Do and end two letters into serious.
explanation.definitionFit: Obese means grossly overweight, a strong medical word for fat.

clue.text: Down-to-earth subject in front of Mercian king and court

blocks.note: subject matter, the topic in hand
Offa was the eighth-century king of Mercia, famous for his dyke
CT is the standard abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A grounded vassal who stands before the Anglo-Saxon king and his courtiers.
explanation.walkthrough: Subject reads as a royal subject, but means topic. Mercia was an Anglo-Saxon kingdom in the English Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: A matter-of-fact person is practical and unemotional, the same plain sensibility as being down-to-earth.
